title: So it isn't lost
hookLine: a teacher dies, his followers split, and Sariputta answers by counting

lines: A TEACHER WITH AN ACHING BACK.
cards: In the town of Pava, the local Mallas have just built a new meeting hall, so new that no teacher has used it yet. They invite the Buddha to be the first.

He comes with his monks and talks with the townspeople late into the night. When they leave, his back aches. So he asks Sariputta, his senior student, to speak to the monks while he lies down on his right side, mindful.
And Sariputta has news from town on his mind.

teach.h: A TEACHER DIES, A COMMUNITY SPLITS
teach.b: Nigantha Nataputta, a well-known teacher of the time, the one Jains remember as Mahavira, has recently died here in Pava, and his followers, the discourse says, have split, arguing over what he really taught, wounding each other with words.
Sariputta says, in effect: let's not let that happen to us.
Let's recite the teaching together, all of us, in agreement, so this way of life lasts long, for the good of many. Then he does what you'd do if you wanted a whole room to remember. He counts.
One thing: all beings are sustained by food. Two things: name and form.

teach.h: ONE, TWO, THREE, ALL THE WAY TO TEN
teach.b: Three: the roots of harm, greed, hatred and delusion. Four: the foundations of mindfulness. On and on, all the way up to ten.
It's the Sangiti Sutta, the reciting together. Tradition says the teaching wasn't written down for centuries; it lived in human memory, passed from mouth to ear.

A number gives the mind a shelf: if you know there are four, you notice when you've only said three. Some scholars think lists like these were one way the early communities kept a huge body of teaching from drifting.
And here's the quiet point. Sariputta's answer to a quarrel isn't a ruling on who was right.

teach.h: SAYING IT TOGETHER KEEPS THE PEACE
teach.b: It's everyone saying the same words, together, out loud.
At the end, the Buddha sits up and says: good, Sariputta, good.

how: Monastics in many Buddhist traditions memorize texts and chant them together, and tradition says the Pali discourses were handed down by recitation for centuries before they were written down.

o: a solo chant for one's own protection
a written copy kept in a monastery

games.q: the reciting together: tap the pairs.
p: all beings are sustained by food

s: DN 33 opens with news of a community splitting after its teacher died
Sariputta hears that the followers in Pava are quarreling and proposes reciting together.
the Buddha recites the numbered lists himself
Sariputta recites them; the Buddha rests and approves at the end.
they climb from ones all the way up to tens.

games.q: you're Sariputta. another teacher's followers have split after his death, and the monks are uneasy. what do you do?
o: warn the monks about that other group.
recite the teaching together, number by number.
name a new leader on the spot.
games.why: he proposes a common recitation, so the community agrees on the words and the teaching lasts.

practice: Learn one short list by heart: the three roots of harm, greed, hatred, delusion, or the five precepts, no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, no intoxicants.
Say it once slowly, counting on your fingers, then again with your eyes closed, and rest on the breath. If it slips away later, that's fine: that's exactly why lists come with numbers.

wordCard.voice: sangiti. Sariputta's reason for reciting the teaching together: so a community stays whole, and the words outlive the people who first heard them. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sangiti: reciting together. the name of DN 33, and later the word for the great councils that recited the canon.

carryVoice: Your line: say it once more. Said together, the words stay whole. Day five hundred seventy-two, done.
